query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy‐alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, the onset and progression of the phase transition during premelting/melting is governed by localized nanoscale melting induced by their high surface-to-volume ratio and limited atom mobility. This transient local liquid formation acts as a mediator that destabilizes the original solid solution and promotes atomic re‐arrangement, thereby triggering the phase transition at temperatures below the bulk melting point.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, disordered (single‐phase) FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles with well‐defined crystallinity and limited atomic mobility.
generation.intervention: Controlled high-temperature exposure with precise heating ramps (varying heating rates and dwelling times) to approach and surpass the premelting regime.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, with strict control of heating rate and temperature uniformity; comparison between samples heated at a rapid ramp versus a slower ramp.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of transient nanoscale liquid domains (localized melting) within individual nanoparticles that serve as nucleation sites for atomic re‐ordering.
generation.mechanism: As temperature increases, the high surface energy and defect density in small HEA nanoparticles lower the effective melting point locally. Limited atomic mobility in the solid leads to an abrupt transition once these nanoscale liquid domains form. The transient liquid state then facilitates atomic diffusion and re‐arrangement, propagating the phase transition (e.g., from a disordered solid solution to a partially reordered or segregated phase) before complete melting occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting fully solid state, nanoparticles that experience localized transient melting will exhibit signs of atom re‐ordering (e.g., phase segregation or structural ordering), changes in particle size (due to coalescence/splitting processes), and distinct thermal response (observable by DSC or in situ TEM). A controlled slowing of the heating rate should delay or reduce the extent of the phase transition due to more gradual temperature homogenization.
generation.baseline: The starting state of the HEA nanoparticles characterized by uniform, crystalline single-phase structure with negligible liquid character as determined by in situ imaging and thermal analysis.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds in the temperature window just below bulk melting (premelting regime) and before full coalescence; beyond complete melting, the mechanism may change due to extensive liquid-phase mixing.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature threshold and kinetics of transient liquid formation, as well as potential influences from nanoparticle size distribution and support effects, remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare batches of FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles and subject them to identical high-temperature treatments under inert atmosphere, with one group heated at a rapid ramp rate and another at a slow ramp rate. Monitor structural evolution in situ using high-resolution TEM and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to detect the onset of transient liquid domains and subsequent phase transformation.
measurements: In situ TEM imaging to capture local melting and atomic re-ordering events
DSC to record subtle endo-/exothermic events associated with localized melting and phase transition
X-ray diffraction to detect changes in crystallinity and possible phase segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no evidence of localized nanoscale melting (transient liquid formation) is observed prior to the onset of a global melt or if variations in heating rate do not produce measurable differences in phase transition onset or nanoparticle structural evolution relative to the baseline state, then the mechanistic hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles. In summary, we report the first synthesis of MPEI nanoparticles with up to eight constituent elements through a unique disorder-to-order phase transition. This transition is achieved by starting with disordered, solid-solution HEA nanoparticles that are Joule-heated for a short period of time (~5 min) followed by rapid cooling (~104 K/s). The HEA starting materials synthesized through a rapid thermal shock (tens of milliseconds heating) enables the mixing of the diverse elements, regardless of their thermodynamic miscibility. The subsequent ~5 min of heating is then critical to achieve the disorder-to-order transition that converts the HEA nanoparticles into MPEI nanoparticles, which is driven by thermodynamic stability. In addition, the limited heating time and the ensuing rapid temperature quenching prevent the MPEI nanoparticles from excessive growth and agglomeration. This unique approach not only produces stable MPEIs at the nanoscale but also can enable previously unidentified MPEI compositions (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn) that have never been achieved by traditional methods because of the inherent immiscibility of the elements.
